all_candidates.g6_note: A trajectory downsampled to 64-128 points x 6 channels in float16 is under 1.5 KB, so 10^6 flights is ~1.5 GB - fits the 30 GB disk with room for the raw pull. Training a small 1D-conv/transformer sequence labeller on 4 cores is fine. The real cost is the OpenSky extraction pipeline (network and query time), not the training; budget for it explicitly.
all_candidates.input_modality: Numeric trajectory tensors: lat/lon/altitude/groundspeed/track/vertical-rate time series, typically 100-500 samples per flight. Pure telemetry.
all_candidates.name: ProcedureNet: recovering coded flight procedures from ADS-B trajectories
all_candidates.one_line: Given a raw aircraft trajectory, recover which published instrument procedure (SID/STAR/approach) was flown and its leg-by-leg ARINC 424 decomposition, including where the crew deviated from the coded path.
all_candidates.output_label: Procedure identifier (extreme multi-class over the CIFP procedure inventory) + per-timestep leg-type label (ARINC 424 path terminators: IF/TF/CF/DF/RF/HM/VA/CA...) + a deviation/vectored-off flag.

all_candidates.g1_corpus: Sentinel-2 L2A and Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel (HLS) via Microsoft Planetary Computer / AWS Open Data (free, CC-BY). Field geometries: USDA Cropland Data Layer + Common Land Unit derivatives, EU LPIS/GSAA parcel registries (several member states publish parcel polygons openly), and the ~2.5 billion open building/parcel-adjacent footprint corpora. Labelled seed: USDA ARS LTAR network, on-farm trial networks, state conservation-district records, and the Operational Tillage Information System (OpTIS) style products.
all_candidates.g1_est_units: US CDL-derived field polygons: UNVERIFIED (widely quoted as order 10^7-10^8 field-seasons). EU LPIS parcels: UNVERIFIED (order 10^7). Labelled seed size from ARS/on-farm trials: UNVERIFIED and small - published studies use 50-500 fields, which is the binding constraint. >=10^6 unlabelled field-seasons is well supported; the seed is the risk.
all_candidates.g2_mechanism: Exactly the VPT shape. Train an inverse model on a small ground-truthed seed (fields where the operator's management records exist) mapping reflectance time series -> management event sequence, then pseudo-label 10^7+ field-seasons of Sentinel-2/HLS history. Strengthen the seed with a shape-(b) component: crop-growth and residue radiative-transfer simulators (PROSAIL + residue mixing models, DSSAT/APSIM for phenology) generate physically-consistent (management -> spectra) pairs for free, which pre-trains the inverse model before the scarce real seed fine-tunes it.
all_candidates.g3_argument: Reflectance time series are not in any language model's input distribution and never will be - plain prompting is not even expressible. The correct scaling story is also strong: management practice is regionally idiosyncratic (residue behaviour under a Midwest freeze differs from the Mississippi Delta), so coverage genuinely improves with corpus breadth, and the label-manufacturing loop is self-reinforcing because pseudo-labelled fields expand the geographic prior.
all_candidates.g3_risk: The 'bigger general model' threat is real but it is not an LLM - it is a geospatial foundation model. Prithvi, Clay, AlphaEarth-style embeddings and their successors are trained on all of Sentinel/Landsat and are explicitly marketed as 'fine-tune on 50 labelled fields for any task'. If a frontier EO foundation model plus a linear probe on the same tiny seed matches the pseudo-labelling pipeline, the thesis dies exactly the way the founder's previous project did. Second risk: G4 is only moderately clear - conservation-tillage and cover-crop detection from Sentinel-2 is an active applied remote-sensing literature (CPSI index at 92% accuracy, cover-crop biomass work in France, South Dakota tillage mapping, plus explicit carbon-MRV framing), so there are arguably >=3 serious efforts already, even though none frames it as a scaling law over manufactured labels. Third: label noise in the seed itself (farmer-reported tillage is unreliable) caps achievable accuracy independent of data volume, which would flatten the scaling curve for reasons that have nothing to do with the thesis.
all_candidates.g5_buyer: Agricultural carbon-credit MRV registries and their buyers (Verra, Indigo Ag, Bayer Carbon, Agoro) plus USDA RMA crop-insurance underwriters, both of whom must verify practice claims at field scale and currently pay for attestation.
all_candidates.g6_note: Training is CPU-fine: a field-season is ~40 dates x 10 bands = 400 floats, so 10^6 field-seasons is ~1.6 GB fp32 and a small temporal CNN/transformer trains in hours on 4 cores. The GPU-free claim holds ONLY if you pre-extract time series server-side (Planetary Computer / Earth Engine style zonal statistics) rather than downloading imagery - downloading tiles would blow the 30 GB disk immediately. Flag this as the main execution risk: data acquisition, not training.
all_candidates.input_modality: Per-field multi-band reflectance time series: ~10 bands x 20-70 acquisition dates, plus derived indices (NDTI, NDVI, NDWI) and weather covariates. Small numeric matrices, not imagery.
all_candidates.name: FieldOps: inverse dynamics for farm management events from field spectral time series
all_candidates.one_line: Recover the hidden human ACTIONS on a field (planting date, tillage pass, cover-crop termination, irrigation, harvest) from the field's satellite reflectance time series - a literal inverse-dynamics model where the actions are the labels nobody has.
all_candidates.output_label: Event sequence over the season: {no-till / reduced-till / conventional-till} x date, planting date, cover-crop presence and termination date, harvest date, irrigation events.

all_candidates.g1_corpus: Mobility Database / TransitLand aggregate thousands of open GTFS static feeds plus GTFS-Realtime archives (feed count: UNVERIFIED). Public GTFS-RT archives (e.g. multi-year vehicle-position archives published by several North American and European agencies) give the paired (GPS, known schedule) side. Unlabelled side: raw AVL/GPS traces from informal and semi-formal transit in the global south, collected in projects like DigitalMatatus/DigitalTransport4Africa, plus commercial fleet telematics.
all_candidates.g1_est_units: GTFS-RT vehicle positions in public archives: UNVERIFIED, but a single mid-size agency emits ~10^5-10^6 pings/day, so >=10^9 pings across archives is very plausible. The training unit should be a trajectory segment or a stop-visit, giving >=10^6-10^7 units. Count of GTFS feeds in Mobility Database: UNVERIFIED.
all_candidates.g2_mechanism: Shape (c): for the ~thousands of agencies that publish BOTH GTFS static and GTFS-Realtime, the schedule is the structured source that the observed vehicle motion was generated against - so aligning RT pings to the static feed manufactures exact per-ping labels (which trip, which stop index, which pattern) at zero marginal cost, for free, forever. Shape (a): train the inducer on that free-labelled side, then pseudo-label raw GPS from cities with no feed at all.
all_candidates.g3_argument: Input is a stream of coordinates and timestamps; there is no textual formulation. The learned prior that matters - what a dwell looks like versus a traffic stop, where a stop actually is versus where the vehicle happened to idle, how a pattern branches - is statistical and improves with the number of distinct agencies, vehicle types, road environments and driving cultures observed. That is a clean scale story.
all_candidates.g3_risk: Strongest attack: this is largely a clustering-and-alignment problem and classical pipelines already exist and are cheap - gps2gtfs (an arXiv-published Python package) and 'busbuzzard' do probabilistic schedule inference, and DBSCAN-plus-HMM stop detection is a textbook baseline. A frontier model with a code interpreter will write a competent version of that pipeline in one shot, which is the 'plain prompting eats it' failure at system level. Second, the free-label distribution is biased: agencies that publish GTFS-RT are formal, well-funded, and drive fixed routes on paved roads, while the target population (matatus, jeepneys, colectivos) has no fixed stops and no fixed schedule - so the sim-to-real gap here is a genuine ontological gap, not just a covariate shift, and pseudo-labelling may transfer badly. Third, G5 is soft: the buyers are development agencies and small vendors, not deep pockets.
all_candidates.g5_buyer: Transit-data vendors (Swiftly, Optibus, Trillium, Via) and multilateral development funders (World Bank, ITDP) who pay for one-off manual GTFS surveys of informal transit networks today.
all_candidates.g6_note: Pings are tiny; even 10^7 pings is a few hundred MB as int32/float32. Alignment labelling with a GTFS static feed is pure CPU. Four scales are easy. The only cost is bulk-downloading RT archives, which is bandwidth not compute.
all_candidates.input_modality: Sequences of (timestamp, lat, lon, optional vehicle id) numeric tuples, unsegmented and unlabelled. Trajectory telemetry.
all_candidates.name: TimetableInduction: manufacturing GTFS schedules from raw transit vehicle GPS
all_candidates.one_line: Given only raw GPS pings from transit vehicles, induce the underlying network - stops, route shapes, trip patterns and the scheduled timetable - for the majority of world transit that has no published feed.
all_candidates.output_label: Induced GTFS objects: stop locations, stop sequence per pattern, route/pattern segmentation of each trajectory, headway/timetable parameters, and per-ping trip-and-stop-index assignment.

all_candidates.g1_corpus: Clean text: OSCAR/mC4/Wikipedia dumps in all scripts (freely licensed), plus CJK-heavy sources (Aozora Bunko, Chinese Text Project). Real corrupted corpus: MARC/UNIMARC records in national library union catalogues, EAD finding aids, legacy museum collection-management exports, and the long tail of CSV/XML government data drops that were migrated through Windows-1252 at some point. Codecs: Python codecs / iconv / ICU, all free.
all_candidates.g1_est_units: Effectively unbounded: every (clean string x random corruption chain) is a labelled unit, and clean multilingual corpora are in the 10^9+ document range. >=10^6 units is trivial. Count of genuinely mojibaked records in real library catalogues: UNVERIFIED.
all_candidates.g2_mechanism: The codec library is the label manufacturer and it is exact and free. Sample a clean string, sample a corruption chain of length 1-4 from the codec vocabulary (including lossy hops that produce replacement characters and CJK codepages ftfy refuses to touch), apply it, and you have a perfectly labelled (corrupted bytes -> chain, original) pair at microsecond cost. Realism is calibrated against actually-mojibaked catalogue records.
all_candidates.g3_argument: The input is bytes that are by construction not valid text, so it is the opposite of the web-text distribution. The tail is combinatorially large: chains of length >=3 over dozens of legacy codepages (shift_jis, euc-jp, gb18030, big5, koi8-r, cp1251, cp437) produce an enormous space that only a model trained on many samples can navigate; and crucially, several chains can produce the same output, so the task is genuinely probabilistic and benefits from a learned language prior over the original text.
all_candidates.g3_risk: Strongest attack, and it is strong: brute-force. The codec vocabulary is small (tens of codecs), chains are short, and you can simply enumerate all chains up to length 3, invert each, and score the candidate with a cheap character n-gram language model. That is a few thousand tries per string, runs in milliseconds, needs no training, and is exactly what ftfy's `fix_and_explain` already does for the Latin cases. A frontier model can write that brute-forcer, and can also read common Latin-1/UTF-8 mojibake directly with plain prompting. The moat therefore reduces to (i) CJK legacy chains where ftfy explicitly gives up (VERIFIED: ftfy 'cannot handle the legacy encodings used for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, such as shift-jis and gb18030'), and (ii) lossy chains where information was actually destroyed and only a strong prior can restore it. Whether that residue justifies a funded thesis is the honest open question. Economic tail is also thin.
all_candidates.g5_buyer: Library-systems and digital-preservation vendors (Ex Libris/Clarivate, OCLC, Preservica) and national libraries running catalogue migrations where CJK and Cyrillic records currently arrive unreadable.
all_candidates.g6_note: The most CPU-friendly candidate on this list. Units are short byte strings (<512 bytes); 10^6 units is well under 1 GB. Label generation is a Python loop. Four scales spanning 10^3-10^6 train in minutes to hours on 4 cores. Good choice if execution risk must be minimised.
all_candidates.input_modality: Raw byte sequences (and the mis-decoded codepoint sequences derived from them). Byte-level; the whole point is that the 'text' is not valid text.
all_candidates.name: MojibakeChain: recovering multi-hop encoding-corruption chains in legacy catalogues
all_candidates.one_line: Given a byte string mangled by an unknown sequence of encode/decode mistakes, recover both the original text AND the exact corruption chain - the case ftfy explicitly cannot handle for CJK legacy encodings.
all_candidates.output_label: The ordered corruption chain (e.g. shift_jis -> cp1252 -> utf8 -> latin1) as a sequence over the codec vocabulary, plus the reconstructed original byte string.

all_candidates.g1_corpus: Public PCAP archives: the MAWI Working Group traffic archive, CAIDA anonymised traces (registration required), Wireshark sample-capture wiki, malware-traffic-analysis.net, the ICS/SCADA capture collections (S4, DEFCON CTF, 4SICS/Netresec ICS labs). Labeller: tshark/Wireshark with its very large dissector library (dissector count: UNVERIFIED, order 10^3).
all_candidates.g1_est_units: Individual packets across MAWI daily traces alone are order 10^8-10^9 (MAWI publishes 15-minute daily traces continuously since 2001); exact figure UNVERIFIED. >=10^6 dissected packets is trivially reachable on one machine in an afternoon.
all_candidates.g2_mechanism: tshark is the label manufacturer: `tshark -T json -x` emits, for every packet it can dissect, the exact byte offset and length of every field along with the field's registered type. That is a free, exact, machine-generated annotation over arbitrarily many packets across a thousand-odd protocols. Train on the dissectable protocols; apply to the undissectable ones (proprietary IoT, OT/ICS vendor protocols, game and malware C2 protocols) where no dissector exists - which is the entire commercial point.
all_candidates.g3_argument: Raw bytes are not prompt-expressible, and the generalisation being asked for is structural (how protocol designers lay out headers in general), which is exactly the kind of thing that improves with protocol diversity and packet count. There is a clean scale axis: number of distinct protocols seen, not just number of packets.
all_candidates.g3_risk: G4 is the problem and I will not soften it: automatic protocol reverse engineering is an established sub-field with well beyond three serious efforts - Netzob, Nemesys, NETPLIER (NDSS 2021), BinPRE, 'Network Message Field Type Classification and Recognition for Unknown Binary Protocols' (arXiv 2301.03584), PCA-based segmentation refinement (arXiv 2301.03585), automatic state-machine inference (arXiv 2412.02540) - and several of these already use tshark as ground truth. This candidate probably FAILS the white-space gate as stated. Its only remaining claim is that all prior work is unsupervised per-trace inference on small captures, and nobody has run the supervised-at-scale, scaling-law version - which is a thin differentiator. Separately, unsupervised baselines are strong on the easy cases, and a frontier model plus a code tool will produce a competent entropy/periodicity segmenter. Include this only if the scaling framing is genuinely defensible; otherwise cut it.
all_candidates.g5_buyer: OT/ICS and IoT security vendors (Claroty, Dragos, Nozomi Networks, Armis) who must build protocol dissectors for undocumented vendor protocols before they can inspect the traffic at all.
all_candidates.g6_note: Packets are <=1500 bytes; 10^6 packets is ~1.5 GB raw and much less after truncation to the first 256 bytes. tshark labelling of 10^6 packets is CPU-bound minutes-to-hours. A byte-level CNN/transformer over 256-byte windows trains comfortably on 4 cores at all four scales.
all_candidates.input_modality: Raw packet byte streams (<=1500 bytes per unit) plus inter-packet timing and direction. Binary, explicitly outside web-text distribution.
all_candidates.name: DissectorNet: binary protocol field-structure induction from raw packet bytes
all_candidates.one_line: Given raw packet payloads of an unknown binary protocol, predict field boundaries, field types (length, sequence, checksum, enum, timestamp, address) and record framing - with Wireshark dissectors manufacturing the labels for the known protocols.
all_candidates.output_label: Per-byte-offset BIO field segmentation + per-field semantic type tag + framing hypothesis (length-prefixed / delimited / fixed).

all_candidates.g1_corpus: Danish Maritime Authority open AIS (VERIFIED: ~3 TB of CSV published, one 2018 day ~1.9 GB / ~10 million rows, free at web.ais.dk/aisdata). NOAA MarineCadastre US vessel traffic (VERIFIED: 1-minute-filtered Zstd daily CSVs, 2015-present, free). Labelled seed: EMSA THETIS-MRV (VERIFIED public: annual verified fuel consumption, CO2 and operational efficiency per IMO number for ships >5000 GT calling at EU/EEA ports, published for 2018-2023). Ship particulars from public IMO/registry and open datasets.
all_candidates.g1_est_units: AIS position rows: >=10^10 across DMA (3 TB) and MarineCadastre (a decade of daily files) - the 10M-rows-per-day figure for one Danish day is verified. Distinct voyages extractable: UNVERIFIED (order 10^6-10^7). THETIS-MRV labelled seed: one record per ship-year for ships >5000 GT; exact ship count UNVERIFIED (order 10^4/year x 6 years).
all_candidates.g2_mechanism: The VPT shape with a regulator supplying the seed. THETIS-MRV gives verified ANNUAL fuel/CO2 for ~10^4 ships; AIS gives the complete kinematic history of those same ships. Train an inverse model whose per-voyage predictions must sum to the published annual total (weak supervision / aggregate-constrained learning), then pseudo-label the entire world fleet's voyages - including the >90% of ships and voyages that never enter the EU MRV scope. A shape-(b) component pre-trains it: naval-architecture resistance models (Holtrop-Mennen) plus open propulsion curves generate physically-consistent (speed, draught, sea state -> power) pairs for free.
all_candidates.g3_argument: Input is telemetry; plain prompting is not expressible. The genuine scale story is that fuel burn depends on hull-specific, fouling-dependent, weather-dependent behaviour that only emerges across many ships and many voyages, and every additional ship-year of AIS both adds voyages and tightens the aggregate constraint. Coverage of ship types and trade routes improves monotonically.
all_candidates.g3_risk: Strongest attack is physics, not an LLM: the admiralty coefficient / cube-law approximation (fuel ~ displacement^(2/3) x speed^3) plus a published SFOC figure gives a crude but respectable per-voyage estimate with zero training, and refined empirical models (Holtrop-Mennen + a weather correction) are the industry standard. If a hand-built physical model gets within the noise floor of the annual aggregate labels, the learned model has nothing to sell. Second and more damaging: the supervision is ANNUAL and aggregate - one scalar per ship-year - so the effective label count is ~10^4-10^5, not 10^6, and the scaling curve may be capped by label information rather than data volume, which is exactly the failure mode this study is designed to detect but a bad way to spend the study. Third, maritime AIS ML is not empty (trajectory prediction, anomaly detection, AIS-LLM-style work), though the MRV-seeded fuel-inversion framing appears much less occupied.
all_candidates.g5_buyer: Charterers, shipowners and P&I clubs facing EU ETS maritime and IMO CII compliance, plus the emissions-verification firms (DNV, Lloyd's Register, Bureau Veritas) who are paid to verify these numbers today.
all_candidates.g6_note: After voyage segmentation, a voyage is a few hundred numeric samples plus ~20 static fields - tiny. 10^6 voyages fits in a couple of GB. Segmenting 3 TB of raw AIS CSV does NOT fit the 30 GB disk, so the pipeline must stream-and-discard, or work from a geographic/temporal subset. Flag that as the execution constraint; training itself is easy on 4 cores.
all_candidates.input_modality: AIS kinematic time series (position, SOG, COG, heading, draught reports, navigational status) plus static ship particulars (length, beam, deadweight, engine power, ship type) - numeric telemetry and structured fields.
all_candidates.name: VoyageFuel: manufacturing per-voyage fuel and emissions labels from AIS using the EU MRV regulatory seed
all_candidates.one_line: Train an inverse model that maps a ship's AIS trajectory to fuel burn and CO2, seeded on the EU's publicly published verified per-ship annual emissions, then pseudo-label every voyage of the world fleet.
all_candidates.output_label: Fuel consumption and CO2 per voyage/leg (regression), plus operational-mode segmentation (laden/ballast, sea passage, manoeuvring, at-anchor, in-port).

all_candidates.g1_corpus: US Census Bureau API (decennial, ACS, CBP, County Business Patterns) and IPUMS microdata - the microdata that generated the published tables is still public. Eurostat and OECD bulk-download tables plus the underlying microdata access. The unlabelled target corpus is the enormous population of orphan statistical tables sitting in PDF reports, national-statistics archives, and government publications with no machine-readable provenance.
all_candidates.g1_est_units: Labelled pairs are generated on demand: every (variable set x geography x filter) query against the Census API or IPUMS microdata yields a fresh exactly-labelled table, so >=10^6 tables is a matter of compute, not availability. Number of published Census/Eurostat tables and of orphan tables in archived reports: UNVERIFIED.
all_candidates.g2_mechanism: The published table is an artifact GENERATED from microdata by a query, and both the microdata and the query engine are still public. Run millions of queries against IPUMS/Census microdata, keep (query, resulting table) pairs, and invert. Layer on the real disclosure-control operators (differential-privacy noise as used in the 2020 decennial, cell suppression, controlled rounding) so the synthetic distribution matches published tables rather than clean aggregates.
all_candidates.g3_argument: With headers removed the input is a bare numeric matrix, and the identifying signal is arithmetic structure: which margins sum, which ratios are consistent with a known population denominator, what the rounding lattice implies, what the suppression pattern implies. That is a structural inference no prompt expresses, and it improves with the number of query templates and microdata sources observed. It also has an intrinsically extreme output space, which is the regime where scale is known to matter.
all_candidates.g3_risk: The honest killer: in the real world the headers are usually right there. If you give a frontier model the table WITH its row and column labels, it identifies the source variables immediately with plain prompting - which means the header-free framing is artificial, and an artificial framing is a fatal tell for a funding thesis. The defensible version is narrower: table LINKAGE and disclosure-risk auditing, where you must decide whether two tables from different publications were computed from overlapping universes (a numeric-consistency question the headers do not answer), or whether a set of published tables jointly reconstructs individual records - the reconstruction-attack question the Census Bureau itself has litigated. That reframing is genuinely valuable but is a different, smaller thesis. Second risk: reconstruction attacks on published tables are already a studied area in statistical disclosure control, so white space is not assured.
all_candidates.g5_buyer: National statistical offices (US Census Bureau, UK ONS, Eurostat) who must audit disclosure risk across their own published table inventories, and the data-harmonisation vendors who sell reconciled cross-country statistical series.
all_candidates.g6_note: Tables are small numeric matrices (typically <10^3 cells); 10^6 tables is a few GB at most and far less if capped. Query generation against local IPUMS extracts is CPU-only. Four scales are easy on 4 cores, though generating 10^6 distinct queries against a rate-limited public API needs local microdata rather than the live API.
all_candidates.input_modality: Numeric matrices of aggregate cells (counts, means, percentages, margins of error) plus structural features (row/column cardinality, marginal consistency, rounding/suppression pattern). Numbers, not headers.
all_candidates.name: TableInverse: recovering the source query behind published statistical tables
all_candidates.one_line: Given a published aggregate statistical table stripped of headers - numbers only - recover the query that generated it: which variables, which universe filter, which geography, which weighting.
all_candidates.output_label: The generating query as a structured object: variable set, cross-tabulation axes, universe/filter predicate, geography level and identifier, weighting scheme, and the disclosure-control operator applied (rounding, top-coding, cell suppression, noise infusion).

all_candidates.g1_corpus: Text side: Unicode-correct multilingual corpora in complex scripts (Wikipedia dumps for Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Arabic, Khmer, Myanmar; AI4Bharat IndicCorp; OSCAR). Font side: Noto (VERIFIED: 210 families covering 162 writing systems and ~64,000 characters), Google Fonts, and vendor fonts. Shaper: HarfBuzz (open, deterministic). Real unlabelled target corpus: Indic and Arabic PDFs in national digital libraries and government e-gazette archives whose text layer is currently unusable.
all_candidates.g1_est_units: Labelled pairs unbounded: every (text line x font x shaping feature set) is a free sample, and complex-script Wikipedia dumps alone provide >=10^7 lines. Noto's 210 families / 162 scripts / ~64,000 characters are verified. Count of unreadable complex-script PDFs in public archives: UNVERIFIED.
all_candidates.g2_mechanism: HarfBuzz is a deterministic environment that supplies exact ground truth for free in the forward direction: shape(text, font) -> glyph run with cluster mapping. Run it over 10^7 text lines x hundreds of fonts and you have exact (glyph run -> Unicode) pairs at zero marginal cost. Then apply the destructive transforms that real PDF producers apply - drop the cluster map, subset and renumber glyph IDs, split runs at arbitrary boundaries, strip the ToUnicode CMap - so the training distribution matches what is actually recoverable from a PDF.
all_candidates.g3_argument: Glyph IDs are font-private integers with no cross-font meaning, so nothing a general model learned from web text transfers. The inversion is genuinely many-to-many (a Devanagari conjunct glyph maps to 3-5 codepoints; a single codepoint may split across two glyphs with a reordered vowel), so a learned language prior over the target script is REQUIRED to disambiguate - which is exactly the kind of task where more data and more compute keep paying. Coverage across scripts, fonts and shaping-feature combinations is a clean scale axis.
all_candidates.g3_risk: Strongest attack: if you still have the font, the environment inverts itself - enumerate candidate strings, shape each with the same font, and match. Combined with a character n-gram model and beam search, that is a training-free solver for a large fraction of cases, and it is what a competent engineer (or a frontier model with a code tool) would build first. The moat therefore lives only where the font is subsetted beyond usefulness, unavailable, or where shaping genuinely destroyed information. Second, this overlaps my GlyphMap candidate closely enough that a reviewer may treat them as one domain - they differ (outline geometry vs glyph-ID sequences; per-glyph vs sequence-level) but they share buyers and corpora, so propose one, not both. Third, for scripts where the glyph shapes are available, rasterise-and-VLM again short-circuits the whole thing.
all_candidates.g5_buyer: PDF-processing and e-discovery vendors (Adobe, Foxit, iText, Relativity) and national digital libraries in India and Southeast Asia whose complex-script holdings currently fail search and accessibility requirements.
all_candidates.g6_note: Glyph runs are short integer sequences (tens of tokens); 10^6 runs is well under 1 GB. HarfBuzz shaping of 10^6 lines is minutes of CPU. A small seq2seq trains at all four scales on 4 cores. One of the cleanest G6 profiles here.
all_candidates.input_modality: Sequences of (glyph ID, x-advance, x-offset, y-offset, cluster index) plus font-level features. Font-internal integer IDs, not characters - about as far from web-text distribution as it is possible to get while still being about language.
all_candidates.name: ShapeInverse: inverting OpenType text shaping for complex scripts
all_candidates.one_line: Given a positioned glyph run (glyph IDs plus x/y offsets, as found inside a PDF or a rendered layout), recover the original Unicode text - the many-to-many inversion that makes Indic, Arabic and Khmer PDFs uncopyable.
all_candidates.output_label: The original Unicode codepoint sequence, including reordered vowel signs, decomposed conjuncts, and ligature expansions (one glyph -> many codepoints and vice versa).

g4_results.domain: Inverse Linking: compile-unit (object-file) partitioning of stripped binaries from raw code bytes, with DWARF-manufactured labels
g4_results.g4_reasoning:
G4 requires fewer than ~3 serious efforts AND no open dataset at >=10^6 labelled pairs. Both halves fail, decisively.

SEVEN serious efforts, four of them in the last 24 months. The task has a canonical 2018 formulation (BCD, AsiaCCS), a productized commercial prior-art line (SourceDNA patents 9,223,554 / 10,203,968, which literally claim recovering 'boundaries between sets of functions grouped by source code file' and 'the number, order, and relative sizes of linker objects'), a 2022-2023 SE/security line (ModX ICSE'22, LibAM TOSEM'23), and a named 2025 paper doing exactly the headline task with released tooling (REcover, JCVHT 21(1):29, github.com/huku-/recover, 74 stars).

Worse, the SPECIFIC bet — DWARF as the free label manufacturer for a learned binary partitioner — has already been made twice by the same group. Jia et al., 'Towards an Oracle for Binary Decomposition Under Compilation Variance' (arXiv 2506.19425, ACM TOSEM 2025) builds precisely the proposed pipeline (parse debug info with pyelftools, derive binary-to-source function mappings, define ground-truth partition communities) and RELEASES the labelled dataset: 100,768 binaries and 43,312,875 labelled functions across 17 compilers, 6 optimization levels and 4 architectures. That is an open dataset at roughly 43x the 10^6 target-scale bar, published eight months before this check. The G4 'no open dataset at target scale' condition is not marginally violated; it is violated by more than an order of magnitude.

And the learned-model version shipped two weeks before this check. N2NMatcher (arXiv 2608.10043, submitted 10 Aug 2026, same group) trains a hierarchical GNN over ACFG+FCG supervised by DWARF debug-line source labels to decompose stripped binaries into source-corresponding modules, with 855,226 debug-line-labelled FCG nodes and code released. The proposal's novelty claim — 'no circularity, labels come from the symbol table, not the heuristic baseline' — is exactly N2NMatcher's and the Oracle paper's design.

There is also an entrenched non-academic incumbent that no literature search would have surfaced but that matters for the economic tail: the console-decompilation practitioner community (encounter/decomp-toolkit, ethteck/splat) has spent thousands of hours on hand-tuned object-file splitting heuristics for exactly this problem.

One genuinely thin sliver survives: nobody found doing END-TO-END raw-byte-window prediction of the CU partition without an FCG/disassembly front-end, and nobody predicting a coarse source-IDENTITY class per unit as a headline task. But that sliver sits inside a dense, well-funded, actively-publishing cluster with a released 43M-unit labelled dataset — it is a delta on existing work, not white space, and a reviewer or investor would immediately point at Jia et al. 2025/2026.

Separately, and worth flagging even though it is outside G4's scope: the ICF/LTO search turned up a correctness threat to the premise. Identical code folding removes ~10% of functions and link-time optimization dissolves CU boundaries entirely, so for LTO/ICF builds the DWARF CU partition does not correspond to any recoverable byte-level partition — the label manufacturer is not clean on precisely the modern optimized binaries that make the problem commercially interesting. N2NMatcher's entire framing (inlining-resilience) exists because this failure mode is already known to be the hard part.
open_checkpoints: No public checkpoint for compile-unit / object-file partition prediction was found.
N2NMatcher (arXiv 2608.10043) releases implementation at https://github.com/island255/N2NMatcher; whether trained weights are included was not verified in this session.
REcover (https://github.com/huku-/recover) ships heuristic estimators, not a learned model — no weights.
Adjacent stripped-binary recovery checkpoints are abundant and public (LLM4Decompile, DIRTY, ReSym, XDA), which sets an easy transfer-learning starting point for anyone entering this task.

searches.result_summary: Top hit is REcover: towards recovering object files from stripped binary executables (Karamitas & Kehagias, Journal of Computer Virology and Hacking Techniques 21(1):29, 2025) https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11416-025-00565-1 — explicitly 'novel techniques for estimating the number as well as the boundaries of compile-units in binary executables'. Also XDA (NDSS 2021, arXiv 2010.00770) and classic function-boundary-detection work (Shin et al. 'Recognizing functions in binaries with neural networks', USENIX Sec 2015). The exact target task already has a named 2025 paper.

searches.result_summary: REcover again, plus SourceDNA/Apple patents US 9223554 and US 10203968 'Recovering source code structure from program binaries' (https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/9223554) which claim recovery of 'boundaries between sets of functions grouped by source code file or static library' and 'the number, order, and relative sizes of linker objects'. Confirms a sustained research line ending on this exact problem in 2025, not a one-off.

searches.result_summary: BCD: Decomposing Binary Code Into Components Using Graph-Based Clustering, Karande, Chandra, Lin, Caballero, Khan, Hamlen, AsiaCCS 2018, https://software.imdea.org/~juanca/papers/bcd_asiaccs18.pdf and https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3196494.3196504. searches.result_summary: No ML work found on CU recovery under ICF/LTO specifically — only compiler-side literature (gold ICF, GCC LTO, Google Safe ICF). n_relevant_hits counts only the confirmation that ICF folds ~10% of functions and LTO dissolves CU boundaries, which is a correctness threat to the label manufacturer itself: under -flto the DWARF CU partition no longer corresponds to a recoverable byte-level partition.

serious_efforts.name: BCD: Decomposing Binary Code Into Components Using Graph-Based Clustering (Karande, Chandra, Lin, Caballero, Khan, Hamlen)
serious_efforts.scale: 25 C++ binary programs; heuristic, no learning
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Foundational formulation of the exact proposed task: build a decomposition graph over functions with code-locality, data-reference and call-graph edges, then modularity-optimizing community detection to recover the source-level component/compile-unit partition of a stripped binary. Evaluated against source-level ground truth.

serious_efforts.name: ModX: binary-level partially imported third-party library detection via program modularization and semantic matching (Yang, Xu et al., ICSE 2022)
serious_efforts.scale: Hundreds of binaries; heuristic clustering
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Program modularization of binaries into functionality-coherent modules via Louvain modularity clustering over the FCG, then semantic matching to attribute modules to source libraries. Same partition-the-binary primitive, applied to SCA/SBOM.

serious_efforts.name: LibAM: An Area Matching Framework for Detecting Third-Party Libraries in Binaries (Li, Wang et al., ACM TOSEM 2023)
serious_efforts.scale: Large multi-arch TPL benchmark; GNN-assisted
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Connects isolated functions into 'function areas' over the FCG (i.e. learned/derived binary decomposition) and matches areas across binaries to attribute reused code regions, robust to optimization level and architecture.

serious_efforts.name: REcover: towards recovering object files from stripped binary executables (Karamitas & Kehagias, J. Computer Virology and Hacking Techniques 21(1):29)
serious_efforts.scale: DeepBinDiff/coreutils-scale evaluation; heuristic estimators + modularity fitness + brute-force optimization; tool at 74 GitHub stars
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Directly the proposed task. Estimates the NUMBER and the BOUNDARIES of compile-units in stripped binaries, reconstructs relocation tables so extracted object files can be re-linked with off-the-shelf linkers, and demonstrates CU-structure diffing of Windows kernel images. Open-source IDAPython + CLI prototype released.

serious_efforts.name: Towards an Oracle for Binary Decomposition Under Compilation Variance (Ang Jia, He Jiang, Zhilei Ren, Xiaochen Li, Zhipeng Yang, Yaxin Duan, Ming Fan, Ting Liu) — ACM TOSEM 2025 / arXiv 2506.19425
serious_efforts.scale: 100,768 binaries, 43,312,875 functions, 187,959,002 calls; 17 compilers x 6 optimizations x 4 architectures; 51 GNU projects
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Builds exactly the proposed G2 label manufacturer at scale: DWARF/debug-symbol-derived binary-to-source function mappings used to define ground-truth decomposition communities (Minimal Equivalent Function Regions) across compilation variance, then benchmarks existing decomposers. Releases the oracle construction toolchain, the labelled dataset, and the evaluation framework.

serious_efforts.name: N2NMatcher: Towards Inlining-Resilient Binary Decomposition and Module Matching (Ang Jia, He Jiang, Zhipeng Yang, Zhilei Ren, Xiaochen Li), arXiv:2608.10043
serious_efforts.scale: 3,024 x86-64 binaries, 84 targets, 28 projects; 1,403,680 FCG nodes / 7,417,670 edges; 855,226 nodes with debug-line source labels; plus ISRD set of 608 stripped binaries
serious_efforts.what_it_did: A LEARNED binary decomposer supervised by DWARF debug-line source labels — i.e. the proposed thesis, already executed. Hierarchical GNN encoding ACFG+FCG with calling context, predicts inlining-stable anchor functions, decomposes and matches modules. Handles the function-inlining failure mode that breaks source-level partition labels. Code released.

serious_efforts.name: SourceDNA (acquired by Apple) — US Patents 9,223,554 and 10,203,968, 'Recovering source code structure from program binaries'
serious_efforts.scale: Productized at app-store scale; method undisclosed beyond claims
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Commercial prior art claiming recovery, from symbol-free and debug-free executables, of 'boundaries between sets of functions grouped by source code file or static library', function scope/visibility, and 'the number, order, and relative sizes of linker objects'. Encumbers the commercial tail of the thesis.

g4_results.domain: Compressed-stream encoder provenance: identifying the encoder implementation, version bucket and parameter tuple from raw DEFLATE/zstd/brotli/LZMA bitstream bytes, precisely enough to recompress byte-identically
g4_results.g4_reasoning:
ZERO machine-learning efforts exist on this exact task, and NO labelled dataset exists at any scale, let alone 10^6. The searches were consistent and unambiguous across every venue.

HARD NEGATIVES (the strongest evidence):
- arXiv: "compressor identification deflate encoder" -> literally "produced no results". "'compressed stream' classification encoder parameters" -> "produced no results". A bare "deflate" search returns 40 hits that are almost entirely numerical-linear-algebra *matrix deflation* plus unrelated LLM papers; the single hit mentioning DEFLATE (arXiv:2606.18900) is about GPU decode throughput.
- GitHub repository search via the API, three separate query formulations ("deflate compression level detection identify encoder", "zlib compression level fingerprint recompress byte identical", "deflate parameter detection encoder provenance compressed stream classifier"): total_count = 0, 0, and 0.
- HuggingFace datasets, search "deflate": four hits, all irrelevant (a video-effect LoRA dataset and three LLM distillation sets). No compressed-stream corpus labelled with encoder or parameters exists.
- DCC (Data Compression Conference, the field's own venue): no paper on identifying a compressor from its output.
- DFRWS (digital forensics venue): multiple query formulations returned zero work on compressor attribution. The forensics literature that does exist is a DIFFERENT task -- EnCoD (arXiv:2010.07754) and "Reliable Detection of Compressed and Encrypted Data" (arXiv:2103.17059, De Gaspari et al. 2021) distinguish *compressed vs encrypted* fragments and identify *file format*, explicitly NOT which encoder implementation or level produced the bytes. I verified this by fetching 2103.17059 directly.

WHAT DOES EXIST (four non-ML heuristic tools at an ADJACENT problem -- byte-identical *reconstruction*, not *identification*):
1. precomp (schnaader) -- brute-forces zlib's three parameters; per preflate's own README it only works for streams made by the zlib library itself.
2. preflate / microsoft/preflate-rs -- splits a stream into data + reconstruction diff. It attempts zlib level detection but its README concedes it emits >3 bytes of reconstruction data for 20-30% of zlib streams, i.e. its heuristic identification fails a quarter of the time. No ML.
3. google/grittibanzli -- archived June 2022; explicitly encoder-AGNOSTIC by design, storing "deflate choices" so it never has to identify the encoder. No ML.
4. reproducible-apk-tools/list-compresslevel.py (Stegerman, 2024) -- detects level by brute-force trial recompression and CRC32 comparison, within a single ASSUMED implementation. Cannot distinguish zlib vs zlib-ng vs libdeflate vs zopfli vs 7-Zip vs Java Deflater.

Critically, these tools STRENGTHEN rather than weaken the thesis. They are hand-written heuristics that solve a different problem (store the diff) precisely because identification was too hard, and they demonstrably break on real inputs. The September 2024 reproducible-builds mailing list thread "unreproducible zlib/deflate compression in ZIP/APK files" is the smoking gun: Fay Stegerman reports that after Fedora shipped zlib-ng as the system zlib, APKs stopped rebuilding reproducibly and Google's patching algorithm broke. When I fetched the thread I confirmed that NO existing tool is named for identifying which implementation produced a stream; the only thing anyone had was her own experimental script trying "every possible combination of parameters", which still failed to reproduce upstream APKs. That is an unsolved, actively painful problem with a named community asking for exactly this capability.

CALIBRATION -- why I am confident this is white space and not a dead end: the *identical problem shape on a neighbouring artifact* is a well-developed field. Compiler/toolchain provenance recovery from binaries (which compiler family, version, optimization level produced this code) has Rosenblum & Miller ISSTA 2011, o-glassesX at NDSS BAR 2020, BinProv at RAID 2022, Du et al. at USENIX ATC 2022, and a CCS 2023 paper on using compiler provenance for security tasks. So the research community has validated that "recover the generator's settings from the generated artifact via learning" is a real, publishable, useful problem -- it has simply never been pointed at compressed bitstreams. The one adjacent learned-classification result I found is audio codec classification from variable-bitrate streams (Digital Signal Processing / Elsevier, ~2020), a different modality and a coarser label space (which codec format, not which implementation + level + strategy).

NUANCE I WANT ON THE RECORD: a strict reader could count the four reconstruction tools as "3-5 efforts" and argue MARGINAL. I call PASS because (a) none of them is a learning effort, (b) none predicts encoder *implementation* -- the label that actually matters here, (c) two of them are explicitly designed to AVOID identification, and (d) there is no dataset and no benchmark whatsoever, so there is nothing to be scooped by and nothing to compete against. The white space is the ML formulation plus the corpus, which is exactly the FDM-1 pattern.

G4 PASSES: zero serious efforts at the actual thesis, no open dataset at target scale.

searches.result_summary: HIGH VALUE - found the four adjacent tools. microsoft/preflate-rs and deus-libri/preflate (split deflate into data + reconstruction info); google/grittibanzli; schnaader/precomp-cpp. Key distinction surfaced: precomp does bit-correct reconstruction efficiently but ONLY for zlib-library streams needing 3 zlib parameters, whereas grittibanzli reconstructs ANY deflate stream by storing choices in an uncompressed byte format. So the ecosystem bifurcates into (a) brute-force zlib-only parameter search and (b) encoder-agnostic diff storage. Nobody learns encoder identity.

serious_efforts.name: precomp / precomp-cpp (schnaader)
serious_efforts.scale: Per-stream brute force over ~3 zlib parameters; single assumed implementation
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Recompresses already-compressed files by decompressing embedded deflate streams and brute-force searching zlib's three relevant parameters until re-compression is bit-identical; if found, stores the decompressed data plus the parameters instead of the stream. This is the closest thing to the thesis that exists, but it is exhaustive search rather than inference, and per preflate's own README it does bit-correct reconstruction 'only for deflate streams created by the ZLIB library'. No machine learning, no encoder-implementation classification, no dataset.

serious_efforts.name: preflate / microsoft/preflate-rs
serious_efforts.scale: Production library (used for PDF/PNG/ZIP/docx recompression); no training data, no benchmark
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Splits a deflate stream into uncompressed data plus reconstruction information, and rebuilds the original from the two. It attempts zlib compression-level detection, but the README concedes precomp had better zlib level detection and that preflate emits more than 3 bytes of reconstruction data for roughly 20-30% of zlib streams, i.e. its hand-written identification heuristic fails on about a quarter of real inputs. Handles 7zip and kzip streams by storing larger diffs rather than by identifying them. No ML. This is the strongest evidence that heuristic identification is inadequate and that a learned approach is unexplored.

serious_efforts.name: google/grittibanzli
serious_efforts.scale: Archived research tool; no dataset, no model
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Decomposes a deflate container into uncompressed data, the 'deflate choices' needed to reproduce the exact stream, and container metadata, then compresses each independently with Brotli/PPMd. Explicitly designed to be encoder-AGNOSTIC -- it reproduces the stream 'no matter what deflate compressor was used' precisely so it never has to identify the encoder. Its 'prediction' is algorithmic, not ML. Compresses the choices stream by only 0.5-1% for high-quality gzip. Archived and unmaintained. Counts as a serious engineering effort at the adjacent reconstruction problem, and as direct evidence that Google chose diff-storage because identification was not tractable by hand.

serious_efforts.name: reproducible-apk-tools / list-compresslevel.py (FC 'Fay' Stegerman)
serious_efforts.scale: Per-entry brute force over ~10 levels, one implementation; no dataset, no model
serious_efforts.what_it_did: The only published detector. Determines the compression level of a ZIP/APK entry by recompressing the data at each candidate level and comparing the CRC32 of the result against the CRC32 of the original compressed data. Brute force, and critically it assumes a single implementation (Python's zlib), so it cannot distinguish zlib from zlib-ng, libdeflate, zopfli, 7-Zip, Apple's fork or Java Deflater. On the rb-general list Stegerman reports her exhaustive 'every possible combination of parameters' variant still failed to reproduce upstream APKs. Defines the state of the art and its exact failure boundary.

g4_results.domain: JVM bytecode build-provenance: predicting compiler implementation/version, build tool, and compile flags from .class bytecode alone, and flagging artifacts whose bytecode contradicts declared provenance
g4_results.g4_reasoning:
Across 15 searches spanning arXiv (search UI, cs.SE monthly listing, and direct abs fetches — the export API 429'd), general web, GitHub repo search, the HuggingFace datasets API, Papers-with-Code, and four domain-specific venues (ACM CCS SCORED supply-chain workshop, ICSE/ICSE-SEIP, MSR + Zenodo, and the Reproducible Builds / Apache Maven practitioner community), I found ZERO efforts that train any model to predict the compiler implementation, point version, build tool, or compile flags from JVM .class bytecode, and zero that frame 'bytecode contradicts declared provenance' as a learned detection task on JVM artifacts.

What exists is three adjacent efforts, and the shape of their adjacency is unusually favourable. (1) APKiD is the same idea executed by hand: YARA rules that fingerprint the DEX compiler from map-type ordering, used precisely as a repackaging/tamper signal. It proves the label is economically meaningful and that the structural signal is real — but it is rules, on DEX, with ~6 classes and no versions or flags. (2) The Dietrich/Hassanshahi group (VUW + Oracle Labs) and (3) the Sharma/Baudry/Monperrus group (KTH) both build multi-JDK Java class-file corpora and both hand-enumerate exactly which bytecode features vary with Build-Jdk-Spec — and then spend the entire paper trying to NORMALISE THAT SIGNAL AWAY so two builds can be declared equivalent. Nobody has turned around and asked the model to read the signal instead. That is a genuine inversion, not a gap in coverage. The Java Decompiler Diversity paper (arXiv 2005.11315) independently notes javac and ecj emit different synthetic wrappers for identical source, again as an observation nobody exploits.

No open dataset comes near the 1e6 target with the right label. The largest open multi-compiler Java corpus is BinEq at 622,029 pairs — under half the threshold, and its label is binary equivalence, not toolchain identity. DALEQ's eval is 265,690 class pairs. Reproducible Central is ~5k releases. Goblin's 16.2M releases are a metadata graph with no bytecode. HuggingFace returns literally zero. Kaggle returns nothing. There is no checkpoint of any kind.

Two honest caveats that keep this from being a 0-crowding call. First, the native-binary analogue is saturated — Rosenblum 2010, BinProv (RAID'22), NeuralCI, MuCPI, vision-transformer variants, Assemblage, ICSE-SEIP'24 'The Devil Is in the Command Line' — and the EVM analogue is done too (VSmart, the Wright State thesis). A reviewer will say 'this is BinProv on the JVM'. Under the FDM-1 pattern that is acceptable, because the novelty is supposed to be the manufactured corpus rather than the method — but it is not an unclaimed formulation, only an unclaimed corpus. Second, the two groups sitting on the adjacent corpus are well-resourced (Oracle Labs, KTH) and already have jcompile, the JDK matrix, and the feature taxonomy in hand; the pivot cost from 'canonicalize the difference' to 'classify the difference' is low, so the white space is real today but not structurally defended.

Separately, and outside G4's remit but worth flagging to the parent: the label design has a soundness hazard the crowding check surfaced. major_version in the class header trivially encodes -target, so that head is free and uninteresting; MANIFEST Build-Jdk records the JDK that ran Maven, not necessarily the -release actually used; and javac point releases within a major version frequently emit byte-identical output, so the 'point version' head may be near-unlearnable on the harvested slice and would need the Docker recompilation matrix to be the primary manufacturer rather than the fallback. This affects G2/G3 quality, not G4.

Fewer than 3 serious efforts in the actual domain (arguably one, APKiD, and it is on a different bytecode format), and no open dataset at target scale. G4 PASSES.

searches.query: arXiv 2410.08427 'Levels of Binary Equivalence for the Comparison of Binaries from Alternative Builds'; arXiv 2504.21679 'Causes and Canonicalization of Unreproducible Builds in Java'; arXiv 2508.01530 'DALEQ - Explainable Equivalence for Java Bytecode'
searches.result_summary: All three real and directly adjacent, none doing the task. 2410.08427 (Dietrich, White, Hassanshahi, Krishnan; Oct 2024/rev Apr 2025): 14,156 Java binary pairs from independent providers (Google/Oracle/RedHat rebuilds); 26.49% of jar pairs differ in >=1 class file; proposes equivalence LEVELS; explicitly no ML, no compiler label. 2504.21679 (Sharma, Baudry, Monperrus; IEEE TSE 2025): taxonomy of 6 root causes of unreproducibility, Chains-Rebuild on 12,803 unreproducible artifacts, canonicalization via jNorm + OSS-Rebuild; explicitly notes Build-Jdk-Spec differences cause both MANIFEST and .class bytecode differences; no ML. 2508.01530 (Dietrich et al., Aug 2025): DALEQ disassembles bytecode into a relational DB and normalises with datalog rules; evaluated on 2,714 JAR pairs / 265,690 class pairs; symbolic, no ML. Crucially all three aim to CANCEL the toolchain signal, the exact inverse of the proposed thesis.

serious_efforts.name: APKiD (RedNaga) — rule-based compiler fingerprinting for Android DEX
serious_efforts.scale: ~a few dozen hand-written YARA rules; 2,562 GitHub stars
serious_efforts.what_it_did: YARA rules (apkid/rules/dex/compilers.yara) that identify which compiler produced a DEX file — dx, dexmerge, dexlib 1.x, dexlib 2.x — chiefly from DEX map-type ordering, which the spec leaves undefined. Used exactly as the proposed primary head: a dexlib fingerprint implies the app was decompiled and repackaged, i.e. its bytecode contradicts its declared provenance. This is the closest thing to the thesis that exists, but it is hand-written rules, on DEX not JVM .class, targets ~6 compilers with no version/flag granularity, and involves no learning and no dataset.

serious_efforts.name: BinEq / Levels of Binary Equivalence / DALEQ / jcompile (Dietrich, Hassanshahi, White, Krishnan — Victoria Univ. Wellington + Oracle Labs)
serious_efforts.scale: 622,029 labelled pairs (equivalence label); 265,690 class pairs in the DALEQ eval; ~1e5–1e6 units but wrong label
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Owns the corpus next door but frames the inverse task. jcompile compiles Java projects under a matrix of compilers/JDKs; BinEq (SCORED'24) releases 622,029 binary pairs labelled equivalent/not; 'Levels of Binary Equivalence' (arXiv 2410.08427) compares 14,156 pairs of jars independently built by Google/Oracle/RedHat and finds 26.49% differ in at least one class file; DALEQ (arXiv 2508.01530) disassembles bytecode into a datalog relational DB and normalises it, evaluated on 2,714 jar pairs / 265,690 class pairs. Every artefact is aimed at ERASING the toolchain fingerprint so two builds can be declared equivalent. No ML anywhere, no compiler-identity label, no attempt to predict provenance.

serious_efforts.name: Chains-Rebuild / jNorm / 'Causes and Canonicalization of Unreproducible Builds in Java' (Sharma, Baudry, Monperrus — KTH)
serious_efforts.scale: 12,803 artifacts canonicalized; 4,956 releases analysed
serious_efforts.what_it_did: Empirical taxonomy of six root causes of Java build unreproducibility over the Reproducible Central dataset (706 projects, 4,956 releases; Oct 2024 snapshot), then canonicalizes 12,803 unreproducible artifacts with jNorm + OSS-Rebuild, succeeding on 26.60%. Explicitly documents that Build-Jdk-Spec differences explain both MANIFEST.MF and .class bytecode divergence — i.e. it hand-enumerates precisely the feature the proposed model would learn. Rule-based and taxonomic; trains nothing.

g4_results.domain: Headerless load-layout recovery: base address, ISA and section segmentation for raw firmware blobs
g4_results.g4_reasoning: The domain splits cleanly into two halves with opposite crowding, and the proposal bundles them. (1) THE ISA + CODE/DATA HALF IS CROWDED — I count five to six serious learned efforts: ELISA (DIMVA 2018) already does ISA identification AND code/data section segmentation on raw headerless binaries, which is 2 of the 4 proposed labels; ISAdetect (CODASPY 2020) does ISA + endianness + word size and RELEASED a 98,500-binary open dataset across 23 architectures with working code still maintained in 2026; LOADSTAR (IEEE S&P 2025) does code/data separation for headerless binaries using exactly the proposal's structural trick — train on standard binaries where the header supplies free labels, adapt via pseudo-labels — and it is a top-tier-venue paper from twelve months ago; Andreassen & Morrison (arXiv 2410.21558, 2024) does endianness and instruction width for unknown ISAs; cpu_rec (752 stars, updated Aug 2026) is the maintained incumbent for ISA-from-bytes; and Large Byte Model (arXiv 2606.02834, Jun 2026) reports 98% architecture classification directly from raw executable bytes, which is the proposal's own modality moat already being claimed at scale. That is well over the ~3-effort threshold. (2) THE BASE-ADDRESS HALF IS GENUINE ML WHITE SPACE — across fifteen searches on arXiv, GitHub (MCP repo search returned total_count 0 twice), HuggingFace, IEEE S&P, USENIX/NDSS, DFRWS and the practitioner community, I found ZERO learned models that predict a load base address. But it is not an empty field: it is owned by a mature non-ML incumbent stack — five-plus peer-reviewed heuristic papers (Digital Investigation 2016 FIND-LP, IJCIP 2016, Computers & Security 2019 for MIPS, WCMC 2021 function-address matching) and four widely used tools (binbloom v2, rbasefind, basefind2, allyourbase) that already solve the well-formed ARM/MIPS case by deterministic pointer/string-histogram argmax. This is simultaneously the strongest white-space evidence and the sharpest G3 hazard: a learned model must beat a cheap deterministic algorithm that is already correct on the easy majority, and 'more data makes it better' is a harder story against an argmax baseline than against nothing. Supporting white-space evidence that is genuinely strong: no open dataset anywhere carries joint base-address / ISA / entry-point / segmentation labels at any scale, let alone 10^6 — HuggingFace is empty (binary-30k is 30k rows, tokenized, and explicitly has no base address or section boundaries; the eleven 'firmware' datasets are hobbyist ROM dumps); the ISAdetect release is 10^5 and ISA-only; Assemblage's 1.3M binaries are shipped WITH headers with no headerless task ever defined over them; and there is no benchmark or leaderboard for base-address recovery. The practitioner side confirms the problem is unsolved in production — EMBArk issue #174 'Automatically guessing the base address of a firmware image' is still open and proposes only surfacing a list of candidate guesses. G3 note in the proposal's favour: every LLM firmware paper I found (FIRMHIVE arXiv 2511.18438, arXiv 2509.09970, AgentRE-Bench) consumes Ghidra pseudo-code, never raw bytes, so plain prompting is not expressible for this input. Verdict is MARGINAL rather than PASS because three of the four proposed labels are demonstrably occupied by 5+ efforts including a 2025 S&P paper using the identical label-manufacturing trick, and a mid-scale open dataset (ISAdetect, 98.5k) exists for one of them. Verdict is not FAIL because the load-base-address label — the one the proposal itself calls 'the hard one' — has literally zero learned prior work and no dataset at any scale. If this domain is pursued, it must be narrowed to base-address (plus entry point) prediction and explicitly benchmarked against binbloom/basefind2 rather than sold as joint ISA + segmentation recovery.
open_checkpoints: kairis/isadetect — ML ISA + endianness detector, trained models and pipeline, Python, 70 stars, last updated Apr 2026 (https://github.com/kairis/isadetect)

airbus-seclab/cpu_rec — statistical Markov/cross-entropy ISA recogniser with a 72-architecture reference corpus, binwalk plugin, 752 stars, updated Aug 2026 (https://github.com/airbus-seclab/cpu_rec); Rust port trou/cpu_rec_rs, 130 stars
BinaryResearch/centrifuge-toolkit — archived, wraps ISAdetect for empirical byte-level analysis of binary files, 81 stars (https://github.com/BinaryResearch/centrifuge-toolkit)

XDA — masked-LM byte model for disassembly/function boundaries, NDSS 2021, code released (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00770); DeepDi, USENIX Security 2022 (https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec22-yu-sheng.pdf). Adjacent task (header known), but pretrained byte-level binary models do exist.
NO checkpoint exists for base-address prediction of any kind — GitHub repo search for 'firmware base address machine learning binary' returned total_count 0.
LOADSTAR (IEEE S&P 2025) states 'we will share the tool (open source)' but no public repository is findable as of Aug 2026 — treat as unreleased.

open_datasets.name: ISAdetect binary file and object code dataset
open_datasets.size: 98,500 binaries across 23 architectures (~27 GB full binaries, ~15 GB code-sections-only). Labels: ISA + endianness + word size ONLY. No base address, no entry point, no per-offset segmentation.

open_datasets.name: Assemblage (the proposal's own intended corpus — already public)
open_datasets.size: 890k Windows PE + 428k Linux ELF = ~1.3M binaries across 29 build configurations, with PDB/DWARF ground truth. NOTE: shipped WITH headers and labelled for function boundaries/names/source lines; there is no headerless variant, no base-address task defined over it, and no published benchmark using it this way.

open_datasets.name: Assemblage-DeepHistory
open_datasets.size: 73,610 binaries (42,188 PE + 31,422 ELF) from 248 packages, ~442M functions, SQLite index. Function-level labels only.

open_datasets.size: 29,793 binaries, 10.8 GB, distributed as pre-computed BPE token arrays plus 31 static-metadata fields. Explicitly excludes load base address, entry point and section-boundary labels; raw binaries not included.

open_datasets.name: Clemens dataset (used as LOADSTAR's labelled-standard-binary source)
open_datasets.size: Multi-architecture compiled binaries; LOADSTAR extracted only 444 32-bit ARM ELF files from it. Small, ~10^3-10^4 scale.

searches.query: deep learning code data separation binary section segmentation byte-level classifier firmware 2025
searches.result_summary: MAJOR HIT. 'You Can't Judge a Binary by Its Header: Data-Code Separation for Non-Standard ARM Binaries using Pseudo Labels' (LOADSTAR), Benkraouda, Diwan, Wang, IEEE S&P 2025, https://hbenkraouda.web.illinois.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/sp2025-loadstar.pdf — I read the full 19-page PDF. Trains a classifier on labelled STANDARD binaries and pseudo-label-adapts it to headerless non-standard PLC binaries. Scale is tiny: 444 32-bit ARM ELF files / 20M instructions (from the Clemens dataset) for training; eval sets of 65, 201 and 119 PLC binaries. ARM only. Does NOT predict base address, ISA, or entry point — code/data only. Also surfaced 'Recognizing the Data Type of Firmware Data Segments With Deep Learning' (IEEE Access 2020) and arXiv 2511.17573 'Binary BPE: Cross-Platform Tokenizers for Binary Analysis'.
